title: Civilization Is One Flight Away From Ebola
excerpt: One book tells the story of Ebola in full detail — and it spent 61 weeks at the top of The New York Times nonfiction bestseller list.
body:
If you want to understand Ebola, one book tells the story in full detail. It spent 61 weeks at the top of The New York Times nonfiction bestseller list.

## About the Author

Richard Preston (born 1954) is an American nonfiction writer and a contributor to *The New Yorker*. He earned a PhD in English at Princeton University, where he studied under the celebrated nonfiction writer John McPhee. Preston specializes in bringing the techniques of nonfiction narrative to scientific subjects. In 1984 he published his first nonfiction book, *First Light*, a work about astronomy that won the American Institute of Physics science-writing award. Ten years later he produced another classic of science writing, *The Hot Zone*. His account of the origins of the Ebola virus was a huge success and spent 61 weeks at the top of The New York Times nonfiction bestseller list. It earned Preston the Champion of Prevention Award from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; he remains the only person who is not a physician ever to receive it.

## An Excerpt

Charles Monet was a loner. The Frenchman lived by himself in a small wooden house on the private estate of the Nzoia Sugar Factory, a plantation in western Kenya that runs along the Nzoia River within sight of Mount Elgon. Mount Elgon is a huge, solitary extinct volcano that stands beside the Great Rift Valley and rises fourteen thousand feet. No one knew much about Monet's past. As with many foreigners who end up in Africa, it is hard to say why he came. Perhaps he had gotten into trouble in France; perhaps Kenya's beauty drew him. He was an amateur naturalist who loved birds and animals but did not care much for people. He was fifty-six years old, of medium height and medium build, with sleek, straight brown hair, and he was good-looking. His only close friends were women in the towns and villages around Mount Elgon, yet when doctors later came to investigate his death, the women could remember little about him. His job was to look after the factory's water pumps, which drew water from the Nzoia River to irrigate miles of sugarcane fields. He is said to have spent most of his days in the pump house by the river; he seemed to like watching the machines run and listening to their roar.

In cases like his, the details are often hard to establish. The doctors remember the clinical signs, because no one who has seen what a Biosafety Level 4 organism does to a human body can ever forget it; the signs pile up one after another until they bury the person at the bottom. The Monet case holds both cold clinical data and horrifying images, shocking enough to make us step back and blink hard, as if we had looked at a discolored alien sun.

Monet arrived in the country in the summer of 1979, just as the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), which causes AIDS, was finally breaking out of the rain forests of central Africa and beginning its long torment of the human race. The shadow of AIDS had already fallen across humanity, but no one yet knew it existed. The virus was spreading quietly along the Kinshasa Highway, the road that crosses Africa from east to west and passes Lake Victoria within sight of Mount Elgon. HIV is a Biosafety Level 2 organism: highly lethal, but not very infectious. It does not pass easily from person to person, and it does not travel through the air. You do not need a biohazard suit to handle blood infected with HIV.

On weekdays Monet worked hard in the pump house; on weekends and holidays he went out to the forests near the factory. He would scatter food on the ground and watch the birds and animals come to eat. He would sit perfectly still and watch them. People who knew him recalled that he was especially fond of wild monkeys and had a way with them: he would sit holding a piece of food and wait for a monkey to approach, and it would eat from his hand.

At night he stayed at home. He had a housekeeper named Johnnie, who cleaned and cooked for him. He was teaching himself to identify African birds. A colony of weaver birds lived in a tree near his house, and he spent hours watching them build and repair their pouch-shaped nests. Around Christmas, it is said, he brought a sick bird home, and it died in his house, probably in his hands. It may have been a weaver bird, but no one can be sure; it may have died of a Biosafety Level 4 virus, but again no one can be sure. He also made friends with a crow, an African pied crow, a black-and-white bird that people in Africa often keep as a pet. The crow was friendly and clever. It liked to sit on the roof of Monet's house and watch him come and go. When it was hungry it would land on the veranda and walk inside, and Monet would feed it scraps from his table.

Charles Monet went back to work at the pump house. Walking each day through the blackened cane fields, he surely raised his eyes to Mount Elgon, and even when heavy clouds hid the summit he must have felt its pull, like the gravity of an invisible planet. Meanwhile, something was copying itself inside him. Using Charles Monet's body as its host, it was multiplying as fast as it could.

Headache usually begins on the seventh day after exposure to this virus. On January 8, 1980, seven days after a New Year's Day visit to Kitum Cave, Monet felt a throbbing ache behind his eyeballs. He decided to take a day off and rest at home. The headache got worse. His eyeballs hurt, then his temples, and the pain seemed to circle inside his head. Aspirin did nothing, and then his back began to hurt badly. Johnnie was still away for Christmas, so he found someone to fill in. She looked after him as best she could but did not know what to do. On the third day after the headache started, he developed nausea, a high fever, and vomiting. The vomiting grew worse and turned into dry heaves. By now he had become strangely passive. His face lost all animation and set into an expressionless mask, and his eyes stared, fixed, as if paralyzed. His eyelids drooped a little, so that his eyes looked as though they were trying to pop out and close at the same time. The eyeballs seemed frozen in their sockets, and they turned bright red. The skin of his face went yellow, with vivid star-shaped red spots. He was looking more and more like a zombie. His appearance frightened the woman who was standing in for Johnnie. She did not understand what was happening to him. His personality changed, too: he grew sullen and irritable, and his memory seemed to have gone. He was not delirious and could answer questions, but he did not seem to know where he was.

When Monet had missed several days of work, his co-workers grew worried and went to his house to check on him. The black-and-white crow watched from the roof as they went in. They took one look at Monet and decided he had to go to a hospital. He was too sick to drive, so a co-worker took him to a private hospital in Kisumu, a town on the shore of Lake Victoria. The doctors examined him and could not explain what had happened to his eyes, his face, or his mind. Guessing it might be some kind of bacterial infection, they gave him antibiotic injections, but these did nothing.

The doctors thought he should go to Nairobi Hospital, the best private hospital in East Africa. The telephones barely worked, and in any case there seemed no need to call ahead to say a patient was coming. Monet could still walk, and it seemed he could travel alone. He had money, and he understood that he had to get to Nairobi. They put him in a taxi to the airport, and he boarded a Kenya Airways flight.

A dangerous virus from the rain forest can reach any city on Earth within twenty-four hours by plane. Airline routes link every city in the world into a single network. Once a virus enters the network, it can reach any city a plane flies to within a day: Paris, Tokyo, New York, Los Angeles. Charles Monet carried the thing inside him into that network.

His plane was a Fokker Friendship, a small propeller-driven commuter aircraft rated for thirty-five passengers. It started its engines and flew out over Lake Victoria, whose blue water sparkled, dotted with fishermen's dugout canoes. The Friendship turned east, over green hills covered with tea plantations and small farms. Commuter flights in Africa are nearly always full, and this one probably was too. The plane passed over strips of forest, clusters of round thatched huts, and villages with tin roofs. Then the land dropped away in ledges and gullies, and turned from green to brown. The plane was crossing the Great Rift Valley. The passengers looked down at the birthplace of humankind and saw thatched huts scattered inside rings of thorn scrub, with cattle paths radiating out from them. The propellers droned, and the Friendship bounced and shook as it flew through cloud streets, the puffy cumulus clouds that line up over the rift. Monet got airsick.

The seats on a commuter plane are small and crowded, and you notice anything that happens in the cabin. The cabin is sealed, and the air is recirculated. If there is a smell, you notice it at once. You cannot miss a man who is sick. He is hunched in his seat. Something is wrong with him, but you cannot tell what.

He holds an airsickness bag over his mouth, coughs deep in his lungs, and brings something up into the bag. The bag swells. Perhaps he looks around, and you see that his lips are smeared with red slime mixed with black specks, as if he has been chewing coffee grounds. His eyes are the color of rubies, and his face is an expressionless mass of bruises. The red star-shaped spots that appeared a few days ago have spread and merged into large purple blotches: his whole head is turning black and blue. The muscles of his face are sagging, the connective tissue is dissolving, and his face seems to hang from the bones beneath, as if it were coming loose from the skull. He opens his mouth and vomits into the bag, and keeps vomiting. The vomiting really does not stop: his stomach has long been empty, yet he goes on bringing up liquid. What fills the bag is called *vomito negro*, or "the black vomit." It is not entirely black. It has two colors: black specks like tar, mixed into bright red arterial blood. It is a sign of internal bleeding, and it smells like a slaughterhouse. The black vomit is loaded with virus. It is extremely infective and lethal, the kind of substance that frightens military biohazard specialists out of their wits. Its smell fills the cabin. When the bag is full, Monet closes it and rolls up the top. The bag is bulging and soggy and could burst; he hands it to a flight attendant.

When a dangerous virus multiplies in a host, its particles penetrate every part of the body, from the brain to the skin. Military experts would later say the virus had undergone "extreme amplification." This is nothing like a common cold. At the peak of extreme amplification, a drop of the patient's blood no bigger than an eyedrop holds hundreds of millions of virus particles. In other words, the life form that has taken over the host's body is trying to turn the host into itself. The conversion does not quite succeed, and what results is a great quantity of liquefied flesh mixed with virus, a kind of biological accident. Extreme amplification was what was happening inside Monet, and the black vomit was its visible sign.

His whole body looks rigid, as if any movement would tear something loose inside him. His blood is clotting: clots ride the bloodstream and lodge everywhere, until his liver, kidneys, lungs, hands, feet, and brain are clogged with them. In effect, his whole body is having a stroke. Clots build up in the smooth muscle of the intestines and cut off their blood supply. The intestinal muscle begins to die, and the gut starts to turn black. He no longer feels the full force of the pain, because clots in his brain are cutting off its blood flow. The brain damage is wiping out his personality. This is called depersonalization: the spark of life and the traits of character slowly fade away. He is turning into a robot. Small patches of his brain are liquefying. The higher functions of consciousness go first, leaving only the deep parts of the brain stem, the primitive "rat brain" or "lizard brain," still alive and working. You could say that the soul of Charles Monet has already died, and only his body lives on.

The force of the vomiting seems to have burst blood vessels in his nose, and it starts to bleed. Unclotted, bright red arterial blood runs from both nostrils and drips over his teeth and chin. Nothing stops it, because his blood has used up its clotting factors. A flight attendant gives him a handful of paper towels, and he stuffs them into his nostrils, but the blood will not clot and the towels are soon soaked.

If the passenger next to you on a plane suddenly falls ill, you are not going to call other people over to look and embarrass him. You tell yourself he will be fine. Maybe he isn't used to flying. He's airsick, poor guy, and people often get nosebleeds on planes; the air is so dry and thin... You lean over and quietly ask whether he needs help. He doesn't answer, or he mumbles words you can't make out, so you decide to ignore him, though the flight seems never to end. A flight attendant may have asked him too whether he needed help, but deadly viruses of this kind change the way their victims behave, and they cannot respond to kindness. They turn hostile and do not want to be touched. They seem unable to speak properly. They can give their name, but they cannot tell you what day it is or explain what is happening to them.

The Friendship flies through the clouds and down the length of the Rift Valley. Monet slumps in his seat, apparently dozing... Perhaps some of the passengers wonder whether he has died. No, no, he is not dead. He is moving. His red eyes open, and they roll slightly.

It is late afternoon. The sun drops behind the mountains to the west of the rift and throws rays out in every direction, as if it had shattered on the equator. The Friendship banks gently and heads for the eastern wall of the rift. The land rises and turns from brown back to green. The Ngong Hills appear under the right wing, and the plane begins its descent over savanna where zebras and giraffes graze. A minute later it lands at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Monet stirs. He can still walk. He stands up, dripping blood. He walks down the steps onto the tarmac. His shirt is covered with blood. He has no luggage. His only baggage is inside him: a vast load of multiplied virus. Monet has become a human virus bomb. He walks slowly into the terminal, through the building, and out to the curb where the taxis wait. The drivers crowd around him: "Taxi?" "Taxi?"

"Nairobi... Hospital," he mumbles.

One of the drivers helps him into his car. Nairobi taxi drivers like to talk to their passengers, and this one probably asks whether he is feeling unwell. The answer is obvious. Monet's stomach feels a little better. It feels heavy, numb, and bloated, as if he had just eaten a large meal, rather than empty and burning.

The taxi takes the Uhuru Highway toward the city. It crosses grassland dotted with acacia trees, passes factories, goes around traffic circles, and enters the crowded streets of Nairobi. People throng the roadsides: women walk along the dirt paths, men stroll, children ride bicycles, a man sits by the road mending shoes, a tractor pulls a load of charcoal. The taxi turns left onto Ngong Road, passes a city park, climbs a hill, runs past rows of eucalyptus trees, turns onto a narrow road, and drives through a gate with a guardhouse into the grounds of Nairobi Hospital. It pulls into a taxi stand beside a flower stall. A sign on a glass door reads "Casualty Department." Monet pays the driver, gets out, opens the glass door, and walks up to the reception desk, gesturing that he is very sick. By now he can hardly speak.

The man is bleeding; just a moment, a doctor will see you shortly. He will have to wait until a doctor is free, but a doctor will see you right away, don't worry. He goes into the waiting room and sits down.

The waiting room is small, with padded benches. Clear, strong, ancient East African light falls through a row of windows onto a table piled with dog-eared magazines and lays bright squares on the gray stone floor, which has a drain in the middle. The room smells faintly of wood smoke and sweat, and it is full of dull-eyed patients, Africans and Europeans sitting side by side. A casualty department always has people waiting to be stitched up. They wait patiently, holding towels to their scalps or bandages around their fingers, and you can see blood seeping through the cloth. So Charles Monet sits on a bench in the casualty department, looking no different from the other patients except for his expressionless, black-and-blue face and his red eyes. A notice on the wall warns patients to watch out for thieves, and another reads:

**PLEASE KEEP QUIET**

**THANK YOU FOR YOUR COOPERATION**

**PLEASE NOTE: THIS IS THE CASUALTY DEPARTMENT**

**EMERGENCY CASES WILL BE SEEN FIRST**

**IN SUCH CASES, PLEASE WAIT PATIENTLY TO BE CALLED**

Monet sits quietly, waiting to be called. Suddenly he enters the final phase: the human virus bomb goes off. Military biohazard specialists have a phrase for this. They say the patient has "crashed and bled out." More politely, they say the patient has "gone down."

He becomes dizzy and utterly weak, his spine goes limp, and he loses all sense of balance. The room spins. He is going into shock. He leans forward with his head on his knees, and with a convulsive groan he brings up an enormous quantity of blood, which splashes across the floor. He loses consciousness and pitches forward onto the floor. The only sound in the room is a choking in his throat; he is unconscious, but he goes on vomiting blood and black matter. Then comes a sound like a bedsheet tearing: his bowels have opened completely, and blood is shooting from his anus. The blood is mixed with pieces of the intestinal lining. He is shedding his own insides. The lining of his intestines has sloughed off and is pouring out of him with the blood. Monet has crashed and is bleeding out.

The other patients jump up, back away from the man on the floor, and shout for a doctor. The pool of blood around him spreads quickly. The deadly virus has destroyed its host and is now busy pushing out through every opening in his body, "trying" to find a new host.
